title: Rankings and Reactivity: How Public Measures Recreate Social Worlds
extended_summary:
This article examines how public rankings and other quantitative performance measures change the behavior and perceptions of the people and institutions they evaluate. The central question is not whether rankings accurately measure quality, but how measurement itself produces effects through reactivity. The authors develop a conceptual framework for analyzing reactivity in public measures, focusing on two mechanisms: self-fulfilling prophecy and commensuration.

The empirical case is U.S. News and World Report law school rankings and their effects on legal education. The study draws primarily on 136 open-ended interviews with law school deans, administrators, faculty, and other staff across roughly 70 U.S. law schools, supplemented by observations, public documents, admissions data, and additional interviews with students and business school administrators. The context is graduate/professional education in the United States, specifically law schools competing for applicants, faculty, funding, and reputation.

The paper concludes that rankings do more than describe institutions: they reshape them. Rankings influence student applications and yield, affect reputational surveys, alter internal resource allocation, encourage schools to conform to ranking criteria, and intensify attention to small differences between schools. More broadly, the authors argue that commensurative measures simplify complex realities, create new hierarchies, and can become self-reinforcing social forces that reorganize institutions and status systems.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed qualitative/theoretical case study, not an experiment or quasi-experiment. It offers a strong analytic framework and triangulated evidence, but it does not meet higher-credibility causal criteria for an intervention effect estimate.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper has important institutional relevance and documents substantial reactivity in law school rankings, but it does not estimate a measurable effect size for a K-12 intervention. Its implications are broad and conceptual rather than demonstrating direct educational impact on student outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: This is a theoretical/qualitative case study of U.S. News law school rankings and their reactivity, based primarily on 136 open-ended interviews plus triangulating documents and observations. The paper argues that rankings reshape institutional behavior through self-fulfilling prophecy and commensuration, producing resource shifts, changed admissions and recruitment practices, altered organizational identities, and gaming strategies; it does not report a single causal effect size.
finding.measure: Interviews, organizational documents, observed admissions fair interactions, public application/yield data, and comparative evidence on law school ranking effects
finding.study_size: n=136 interviews; plus 17 admissions staff interviews, 92 short student interviews, 30 business school administrator interviews
